extracted.intended_audience: general readers of humorous/essay literature and writers interested in prose, poetry, and social observation
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century humorous essay/lecture combining observations on poetry, diction, truth, and social manners; useful as informal guidance for crafting witty prose and satirical commentary. The text offers norms about poetic craft, spoken diction, truthfulness, and the social effects of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow time for a poem to mature
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem needs time before its sentiment and music harmonize with the reader; parts (words) must 'become acquainted' and the 'drying process' takes place so the poem can 'ring' properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a violin's fifty‑eight pieces require long acquaintance; words are like pieces that must be 'repeated aloud and murmured over in the mind's muffled whisper' until 'the parts become knit together in such absolute solidarity that you could not change a syllable without the whole world's crying out against you.' Do not judge a poem while its 'sheets are damp'—if of true stuff, it will 'ring better after a while.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use oral reading to test poetic music
rubrics_metrics.description: The music of a poem is best assessed and developed by repeating it aloud; oral repetition helps the component words knit into harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical step: read verses aloud, murmur them in the mind; the text insists on repetition until the lines settle. Anti-pattern: judging poetic music from a first, private, or 'damp' reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction reveals social and educational background
rubrics_metrics.description: Single expressions and turns of phrase fix a man's position and reveal his antecedents, education, and social origins immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the text: pronunciations or words like 'haälth' instead of 'How do you do?', calling an entry a 'hall' or a wagon a 'kerridge', saying 'sahtisfahction', 'remember of', or 'stoppin’' betray local or class origins. Use diction deliberately in characterization or public speech because it communicates far more than content alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mannerisms and gestures disclose experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Small habitual movements can reveal past occupations or experiences at a glance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an ex-soldier, when asked 'Strap!' by an officer, will instinctively put his hand to the shoulder where a strap used to be. In writing or observation, include such details to signal history without explicit exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provocative truth will unsettle people—impact is measured by reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Every real thought on a real subject will knock the wind out of somebody; attack or strong reaction is evidence that one has said something timely and significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations: Dr. Johnson: 'I think I have not been attacked enough for it… I never think I have hit hard unless it rebounds.' Expect controversy; lack of attack may signal lack of impact. Anti-pattern: seeking only comfortable, unchallenging remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect controversy to equalize critics' reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Controversy operates like a 'hydrostatic paradox' that levels fools and wise men: in public dispute, all positions may appear similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for conduct: do not be seduced into overreacting to critics. The author suggests refraining from direct replies to attacks in print, recognizing that controversy distorts reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of hospitality and relationships biasing criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical praise and denunciation are influenced by social relationships and hospitality; reviewers who receive favors (e.g., dinners) are less likely to be severe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: exchange of 'oysters' for epithets—'one man has oysters, and another epithets.' Understand that cordial treatment softens criticism; treat purportedly independent praise with skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve truth rather than smoothing it for convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is like a white cube—stable and upright—whereas falsehoods roll easily; timidity, good-nature, and polite-behavior tend to 'round off and polish' the cubes of truth into something resembling falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: resist pressures (timidity, good-nature, politeness) to make truth more palatable at the cost of accuracy. Educational point: children first learn truth through sensory experience before moralizing reasons are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic and correspondent pieces should avoid careless compilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some 'From our Foreign Correspondent' pieces mix improbable statements and careless conflation of stories and geographies, misleading readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: compiling facts carelessly from disparate sources (mixing geography, folklore, and fiction) and selling them to editors who then publish for effect. Practical caution: verify facts and avoid fanciful conflation presented as reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise, character-revealing humorous detail
rubrics_metrics.description: A single well-chosen image or phrase can compress a 'delicious' biography of manners, education, and aesthetics in a brief utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the visitor who calls a Cupid statuette 'a statoo of her deceased infant' conveys a wide social and cultural portrait in one line. For humor and economy in prose, prefer such precise, revealing details rather than lengthy exposition.
